title: The Practices of Cultivated Attention
author: The Walled Garden
summary: The fifth installment of The Walled Garden's six-part series on attention as curriculum turns from theory to the classroom environment. Its starting point is that social media feeds hook users through unpredictability while functioning as prediction engines that know everything about them, leaving children, including a student who reported nearly ten hours a day on devices over the summer, with little chance of defending their attention. The author's thesis is that the antidote to unpredictability machines is a predictable classroom. The piece builds that predictability in three layers. A predictable room means consistent transition signals rather than jarring bells, silencing the teacher's own notifications, and making teacher movement and proximity legible. A predictable rhythm means consistent openings, warned transitions and reliable closings, with the key distinction that the container is predictable, not its contents. Predictable people means reciprocal commitments from the teacher: no interruption outranks a student, responses to questions are consistent, and the teacher keeps enough spare attention to notice quiet needs. The author insists predictability is not about compliance but about handing students their attention back for their own thinking.
points: The author frames feeds as an asymmetry: unpredictable to the user but precisely predictive of the user, so the classroom must offer the algorithm's opposite.
Classroom sound should be expected rather than silent; consistent transition signals and verbal warnings beat bells, and a teacher's pinging laptop imports an unpredictability machine into the room.
Routine is described as stimulus management, with a consistent lesson shape so transitions stop registering as interruptions and students stop watching the clock.
Predictability runs both ways: teachers commit to not being interrupted by notifications or visiting adults, and to responding consistently so students can predict how they will be received.
The goal is explicitly not obedience but freeing students from spending attention on what they cannot control so they can command their own cognition.
quotes: Pick a feed, any feed — TikTok, Instagram, YouTube — and you’ll notice that what extends your session from the five minutes you intended to a loathsome hour and change is its unpredictability. What’s going to appear next?

To add insult to injury, the unpredictability of our feeds exists in a perfect and outrageous asymmetry: TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube are prediction engines, forecasting your behaviour with clinical precision. We cede our time, agency, and attention. They gain oracular knowledge of everything about us.
Silence isn’t the desired alternative, however. Silence is just empty, and it makes every sound that does appear even louder. What we want is sound that our students expect and understand.

When students understand what our proximity means, they don’t have to watch us all the time. The point is that as our presence becomes predictable, they come to know that our objective isn’t to keep a constant eye on them.

Routine is not just a source of comfort and security. In the twenty-first century, it is a temple retreat away from the endless rock concert of the digital world. Routine, in the classroom, is stimulus management.
It’s worth noting that routine is not monotony. What’s predictable is the container, not its contents. When our classrooms have a sense of routine, students arrive knowing what to expect.

Long before a student brings something to me, she’s predicted how I’ll respond, and decided whether it’s worth it. That calculus depends on how I handled someone else’s wrong answer a month ago, or what my face did when another student failed to finish a task.

We build them so that our students stop spending their attention on things they can’t control and start spending it on their own thinking. This isn’t the business of producing obedience. A predictable classroom hands our students their attention back so they can command their own cognition.
